title: Aṇor aṇīyān: the self in the cave of the heart
theme: The self hidden in the heart, source of the senses, worlds and waters; the unborn one and the two unborn; the four-horned bull; Rudra and the golden germ; immortality by renunciation; the small space in the lotus of the heart; the Lord beyond the syllable.

morphology.note: Printed गुहाशयां. The Muṇḍaka parallel reads गुहाशया (nominative plural, with the ‘seven-by-seven’). Bhāskara explains a nominative here with a Vedic ending («‘सुपां सुलुक्’ इति जस आदेशः»), and offers ‘set in the cave so as to lie there’ («गुहायां शयनमभिलक्ष्य निहिता»); Sāyaṇa reads guhāśaya as the Lord who lies in the intellect («गुहाशयः परमेश्वरस्तस्मादुत्पन्नां»).
Printed रसाच्च. Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara gloss the plural rasāḥ, ‘and the saps’ («रसाश्च मधुरादयो»); the Muṇḍaka parallel has रसश्च. The printed form is kept.
A Vedic -ī stem with nominative -īḥ (as in rathīḥ). Sāyaṇa derives it: «पदं तद्वेति गच्छतीति पदवीः».
ajā means ‘unborn’ and also ‘she-goat’; aja ‘unborn’ and ‘he-goat’. Both commentators take the first sense.

translation.literal: Smaller than the minute, greater than the great, the self is set in the secret place of this creature. Free of sorrow, one sees him, the will-less, the greatness, the Lord, through the grace of the Ordainer. From him come forth the seven breaths, the seven flames, the fuel-sticks, the seven tongues; these seven worlds in which the breaths move, set in the secret place, seven by seven. From this come the oceans and all the mountains; from him flow the rivers of every form; and from this all the plants, and the sap by which this inner self, having come to be, abides. Brahmā among the gods, master of words among poets, seer among the inspired, buffalo among beasts, falcon among birds of prey, axe among the trees — Soma, resounding, passes beyond the purifier. One unborn [male], delighting, lies beside the one unborn [female], red, white and black, who brings forth many offspring like herself; another unborn leaves her, her enjoyments enjoyed.
translation.readable: The self is finer than the finest thing and vaster than the vastest, and it lives hidden in the heart of every creature. Whoever sees it — free of the pull of wants, the Lord in his greatness — sees it by grace, and grief falls away. From it come the senses and their flames, the worlds in which living things breathe, the seas, the hills, the rivers, the plants and the sap that keeps the body alive. Among gods it is Brahmā, among poets the master of words, among seers the seer, among beasts the buffalo, among birds the falcon, among tools for the forest the axe; it is Soma, chanting, that outshines every means of purifying. One unborn, red, white and black, bears many like herself: one unborn self clings to her and follows her; another, having had its fill, lets her go.

translation.literal: The swan seated in the bright, the Vasu seated in the mid-air, the priest seated at the altar, the guest seated in the house; seated among men, seated in the best, seated in the order, seated in the sky; born of the waters, born of cows, born of the order, born of the mountains — the order, the great. They poured ghee; ghee is his source; on ghee he rests; ghee indeed is his abode. According to the svadhā bring [the gods], gladden [them]; O bull, carry the offering made with svāhā. From the ocean a wave full of honey rose up; with the low-voiced [one] it attained immortality entire. That which is the secret name of the ghee is the tongue of the gods, the navel of the deathless. We will proclaim the name with ghee; in this sacrifice we will hold it with reverences. May the brahman-priest hear it as it is praised. The four-horned bright one has sent this forth. Four are its horns, three its feet, two its heads, seven its hands; bound threefold, the bull roars loudly; the great god has entered mortals.
translation.readable: He is the sun in the bright sky, the wind in the air, the fire on the altar, the guest at the door; he dwells among people, in holy places, in the rite and in the heavens; he is born in water, in the cow, in truth and on the hills — he is the true, the great. Ghee is poured into the fire: it is the fire’s source, its support, its home. Fire, bring the gods for our offering and gladden them; carry what we give with svāhā. Out of the ocean rose a honeyed wave, and by the quiet utterance it reached immortality. The hidden name of that ghee is the gods’ tongue and the hub of the deathless. We will speak that name and hold it in this sacrifice with bows; may the priest hear it. A bright bull with four horns, three feet, two heads and seven hands, bound three ways, roars aloud: the great god has entered into mortals.

sandhi.rule: venāt → venād before e; ekam before s is printed ekaggṃ (the Taittirīya anusvāra before a sibilant, here doubled).

sandhi.type: t before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: purastāt → purastād before v.

sandhi.type: a + a; m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: na + aparam → nāparam.

sandhi.type: t before a nasal; a + a
sandhi.rule: yasmāt → yasmān before n; na + aṇīyaḥ → nāṇīyaḥ.

sandhi.type: aḥ + a
sandhi.rule: jyāyaḥ asti → jyāyo ’sti (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)).

sandhi.type: i before a dissimilar vowel; visarga before t; a + i
sandhi.rule: tiṣṭhati ekaḥ → tiṣṭhaty ekas; tena + idam → tenedam.

sandhi.type: a + e
sandhi.rule: tyāgena + eke → tyāgenaike.

sandhi.type: t before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: The t becomes d before y.

sandhi.type: visarga before s; saḥ before a consonant
sandhi.rule: paraḥ saḥ → paras sa: the visarga is written s before s, and saḥ drops its visarga before a consonant.

sandhi_exceptions.note: tyāgenaike · amṛtatvam: the a of amṛtatvam is not elided after -e (classical eke ’mṛtatvam); the metre needs the syllable.

samasa.meaning: the one with the golden germ, Hiraṇyagarbha
those by whom the meaning is made certain through the knowledge of the Vedānta

samasa.vigraha: सन्न्यासः च योगः च / सन्न्यासः एव योगः
samasa.meaning: renunciation and yoga; the discipline of renunciation

samasa.vigraha: परः अन्तः परान्तः, स एव कालः

samasa.meaning: become the dwelling of the highest
standing in the middle of the city

morphology.note: As printed. The anonymous commentator divides para + meśma and says m stands for v by Vedic licence («वकारस्थाने मकारश्छान्दसः»), so ‘become the house of the highest’; Sāyaṇa reads वरवेश्मभूतं, Bhāskara परवेश्मभूतं.

Masculine as printed, though gaganam is neuter. Sāyaṇa glosses the neuter «विशोकं शोकरहितं गगनशब्दवाच्यं ब्रह्म»; Bhāskara takes viśokaḥ as the supreme self within the space («विशोकः परमात्मेति यावद्»).
An active ending on the passive stem (classical parimucyante); Bhāskara glosses «सर्वतो मुच्यन्ते».
Imperfect without the augment, Vedic; Bhāskara: «पश्यत अपश्यद्». Sāyaṇa glosses the present «पश्यत साक्षात्करोति».

translation.literal: Placed threefold, hidden by the Paṇis, the gods found the ghee in the cow. Indra produced one [part], Sūrya one; from Vena they fashioned one by their own power. He who is over all, Rudra, the great seer, saw in the beginning Hiraṇyagarbha, first of the gods, being born — may that god join us with auspicious remembrance. Than whom nothing is higher or lower, than whom nothing is smaller or greater: like a tree, unmoving, the One stands in heaven; by that Person all this is full. Not by action, not by offspring, by wealth: by renunciation some attained immortality. Beyond the vault of heaven, set in the secret place, it shines; ascetics enter it. Ascetics who have made the meaning certain by the knowledge of the Vedānta, pure in mind through the yoga of renunciation, all of them, in the world of brahman, at the final end, are wholly released from the highest deathless. The small, sinless, become the dwelling of the highest, the lotus that stands in the middle of the city — there too is a small space, free of sorrow; what is within that is to be meditated on. The sound declared at the beginning of the Veda and established at the end of the Veda — beyond that, as it dissolves into its source, is the great Lord.
translation.readable: The gods found the ghee hidden three ways in the cow: Indra brought forth one part, the sun one, and from the longing one they shaped the third by their own power. Rudra, the great seer above all, watched the golden germ being born before the gods — may that god give us a good remembering. Nothing is higher or lower, smaller or larger than him; he stands like a tree, still, alone in the sky, and he fills everything. Not by works, not by children, not by wealth — by letting go, some have reached the deathless. It shines beyond heaven, hidden in the heart, and those who strive enter it. Seekers sure of the Upaniṣads’ meaning, made pure by renunciation and discipline, are all set free at the very end. In the body’s city stands a small lotus, the home of the highest; within it is a small space free of sorrow, and what is inside that is what to meditate on. Beyond the syllable that begins and ends the Veda, as it fades into its source, is the great Lord.

syntax: Three units of verse. 10.12.26 states the self in the cave (aṇor aṇīyān … ātmā guhāyāṃ nihitaḥ), names what arises from it with tasmāt, atas, asmāt, lists what it is among each kind (brahmā devānām …), and ends on the ajā verse. 10.12.27 begins with a string of epithets in apposition (haṃsaḥ śuciṣad …) and moves into an Agni hymn on ghee (imperatives āvaha, mādayasva, vakṣi; subjunctives prabravāmā, dhārayāmā, śṛṇavat) and the riddle of the bull (catvāri śṛṅgā …). 10.12.28 completes the ghee riddle, prays to Rudra (yo … sa no devaḥ … saṃyunaktu), describes the One with relatives in the ablative (yasmāt), states the means (na karmaṇā … tyāgena), and closes with two meditations: the space in the heart-lotus (tad upāsitavyam) and the Lord beyond the syllable (yaḥ … sa maheśvaraḥ).

ambiguities.note: Here two words: ‘through the grace of the Ordainer’, as Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read it (Bhāskara cites «यमेवैष वृणुते तेन लभ्यः»). The Kaṭha has the single compound धातुप्रसादात्, which can be read as ‘through the clarity of the body’s elements (senses and mind)’; that reading is not taken by the commentators here.

ambiguities.topic: ghṛta, the bull and the four horns
ambiguities.note: Two different readings run through 10.12.27–28. Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator read the ghee as self-luminous brahman and the four-horned bull as the syllable om (a, u, m and the resonance), with three feet as waking, dream and deep sleep. Bhāskara reads the same verses of the sacrifice: ghee as water and rain, the four horns as the four priests, the three feet as the three fires, the seven hands as the seven metres («सप्त छन्दांसि गायत्र्यादीनि हस्तासः»).

Sāyaṇa: at the fall of the body after knowledge, the knowers are released even from the unmanifest (‘the highest deathless’), which the ignorant are not freed from even at dissolution. Bhāskara: having attained the supreme immortal state they are released in every way, and he records others who say all are released together at the end of the world-age («परान्तकाले महार्थोपसंहारकाले सर्वे युगपन् मुच्यन्त इति»).

Sāyaṇa makes immortality the subject: set in the one-pointed intellect, it shines beyond heaven, and ascetics enter it. Bhāskara: what shines above the world of brahman, set in the heart, the ascetics enter.

metre.name: triṣṭubh, with jagatī and anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Bhāskara: «तत्र त्रैष्टुभोऽयमनुवाकः», with the haṃsa verse a jagatī («हंसश्शुचिषदिति जगती») and the last verse an anuṣṭubh («यद्वेदादावित्वनुष्टुप्»). The printed half-verses count 22, 22, 21, 24, 22, 23, 22, 21, 22, 22 (10.12.26); 24, 25, 23, 22, 22, 21, 21, 21, 21, 21 (10.12.27, the first two the jagatī); and 22, 22, 19, 25, 22, 23, 22, 22, 23, 22, 22, 22, 16, 16 (10.12.28, the last two the anuṣṭubh). The commentators do not explain the departures from 22; vowels joined in the print (saptārciṣaḥ, tyāgenaike) and left unjoined (sapta ime, trayo asya) account for some of them.

beginner: This anuvāka gathers some of the best-known verses about the self. The self is smaller than the smallest thing and larger than the largest, and it sits hidden in the heart. Whoever sees it, by the grace of the Lord, is free of grief. Everything comes from it: the senses, the worlds, the oceans, the rivers, the plants. A riddle follows about one unborn mother of three colours and two unborn ones: one clings to her, the other, having had enough, lets her go. Then a hymn on ghee and a mysterious four-horned bull, which the commentators read either as the syllable om or as the sacrifice. The text then says that immortality is reached not by ritual, children or wealth but by renunciation, and it points to a small space inside the lotus of the heart as the place for meditation. It ends with the Lord who lies beyond the syllable om.
analogy: Like a house with a small inner room: the house is the body, the room is the lotus of the heart, and the space inside that room, small only because of the walls around it, is the same space that fills the sky.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It describes the self hidden in the heart and seen by grace; everything arises from it; the unborn one of three colours and the two unborn; the swan who dwells everywhere; a hymn on ghee and the four-horned bull; Rudra who saw Hiraṇyagarbha born; the One than whom nothing is greater or smaller; immortality through renunciation; the small space in the heart-lotus to be meditated on; and the Lord beyond the syllable that begins and ends the Veda.

commentary.q: Why does the anuvāka come here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the previous anuvākas praised meritorious action and blamed forbidden action; this one teaches the truth to a person whose mind has been purified by them («शुद्धान्तःकरणस्य पुरुषस्य तत्त्वमुपदेष्टुमयमनुवाक आरभ्यते»). Bhāskara: this and the next anuvāka describe the supreme self and are used in its worship («परमात्मोपवर्णनत्वान् महापुरुषा राधनायां विनियुक्तौ»).

commentary.q: How is the self in the cave explained?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the cave is the intellect, enclosed by the heart-lotus; to be ‘set’ there means to be known there, not to be contained («विद्ययोपलभ्यमानत्वं नतु बुद्धावाधेयत्वम्»), since what supports the whole world cannot be held. The fitness to see him comes from the Lord’s grace («धाता जगतो विधाता परमेश्वरः, तस्य प्रसादोऽनुग्रहः»). Bhāskara compares the space within the heart to the space outside («यावान् वा अयमाकाशस्तावानेषोऽन्तर्हृदय आकाशः»).

commentary.q: Who are the unborn female and the two unborn?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the unborn female is māyā in the form of root nature («न जायत इत्यजा मूलप्रकृतिरूपा माया»); her colours are fire, water and earth, or rajas, sattva and tamas. Of the two unborn selves, the attached one cherishes her and goes round in births and deaths; the dispassionate one sets her aside by discerning the truth («तां मायां तत्त्वविवेकेन बाधत इत्यर्थः»). Bhāskara reads her as prakṛti, the three guṇas in balance («लोहितं रजः शुक्लं सत्त्वं कृष्णं तम»), and the one who leaves her as the freed self.

commentary.q: What is the swan verse doing here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: it lists the world as the sun, wind, fire, guest and the rest, to show that for one who has given up māyā the whole world appears as brahman («अज्ञानिदृष्ट्या जगद्रूपेण भासमानं सर्वं ज्ञानिदृष्ट्या ब्रह्मैवैत्यर्थः»). Bhāskara says the one supreme self exists in many forms by its different works («कृत्यभेदेन परमात्मैव बहुधा वर्तत इति योज्यम्»).

commentary.q: What are the ghee and the four-horned bull?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator: ghee, from the root ‘shine’, is self-luminous brahman («घृतं दीप्तं स्वप्रकाशं ब्रह्मेत्यर्थः»), its secret name is om, and the four-horned bull is the praṇava with a, u, m and the resonance as horns. Bhāskara reads the verses of the sacrifice: the four horns are the four priests, the three feet the three fires, and the bull roars at the three pressings («त्रिषु सबनेष्व् ऋम्भिर्यजुभिस्सामभिः प्रयुज्यमानैर्महान्तं शब्दं करोति»).

commentary.q: Not by action, by offspring or by wealth — what then?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: by giving up all worldly and Vedic activity, some inward-turned people attain immortality («केचिदेवान्तर्मुखा अमृतत्वमानशुः»). Bhāskara disagrees about what is given up: obligatory rites cannot be abandoned, so it is the fruit of action that is renounced («तस्मात् फलत्यागिनोऽमृतत्वमश्नुवते»), and he cites the Gītā: «यस्तु कर्मफलत्यागी स त्यागीत्यभिधीयते».

commentary.q: How do knowledge and renunciation fit together?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa raises the objection that elsewhere knowledge alone is said to free, and answers that each has its own use: knowledge removes ignorance by revealing the truth; renunciation purifies the mind by turning it from objects («ज्ञानं तत्त्वप्रकाशनेनाविद्यानिवर्तकं त्यागस्तु विषयभोगवृत्तिद्वारा चित्तशुद्धिहेतुरिति पृथगुपयोग उक्तो भवति»). He takes yoga as the stilling of the mind’s activity and cites Patañjali («योगश्चित्तवृत्तनिरोधः»). Bhāskara: sannyāsa is offering the fruits of action to the Lord, and yoga is samādhi («ब्रह्महुताशने आत्महविःप्रक्षेपलक्षणः समाधिसञ्ज्ञो योगः»).

commentary.q: What is the small space in the heart?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: the meditation is for one not yet able to know the truth directly («तत्त्वं ज्ञातुमसमर्थस्यात्रोपासनमुच्यते»). The heart is an eight-petalled lotus; the space within it is brahman, called small only because of its place, like the space in a pot; he cites the Chāndogya and the dahara section of the Brahmasūtra («दहराकाशस्य च ब्रह्मत्वं दहराधिकरणे निर्णीतम्»). Bhāskara: the body is a city, the heart its palace, the space within its innermost room, and the supreme brahman within that is the king to be worshipped.

commentary.q: What is the sound at the beginning and end of the Veda?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: om, which opens the Vedas and is taught in the Upaniṣads; in meditation a is dissolved into u, u into m, and what lies beyond, meditated on as the fourth measure in the resonance, is the great Lord («सोऽयं महेश्वरो विज्ञेयः»). Bhāskara: what is beyond the three measures, the half-measure, is the meaning to be worshipped («यः परो ऽर्धमात्राकालः स प्रतिपाद्योऽर्थ उपास्यः»).

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The commentators read some words differently from the base: वरवेश्मभूतं (Sāyaṇa) and परवेश्मभूतं (Bhāskara) for परमेश्मभूतं; विश्वाधिक (both) for विश्वाधियः; स्मृत्या for स्मृत्यास्; विभ्राजते (Sāyaṇa) for विभ्राजत्. Sāyaṇa’s anuvāka also has verses not in this base between the swan verse and the ghee verse (yasmāj jātā, vidhartāram, madhu vātā), commented on as his seventh to thirteenth verses.

advaita.text: Both read the anuvāka as Advaita. Seeing the Lord depends on his grace, and they quote an earlier teacher: «ईश्वरानुग्रहादेषां पुंसामद्वैतवासना». The ajā is māyā, and the freed self sets her aside by discernment; the swan verse shows the world as brahman to the knower; the meaning made certain by Vedānta is the identity of the individual and brahman («जीवब्रह्मैक्यलक्षणोऽर्थो»); and the dahara-space is brahman, small only by its place («घटाकाशवत्पुण्डरीकस्थानापेक्षयाऽल्पत्वमुपचर्यते»).

schools.disagreement: Bhāskara’s comment is ritual and grammatical in much of the anuvāka (he reads the ghee and bull verses of the sacrifice) where he speaks of the self, he says the whole world of enjoyer and enjoyed arises from it («भोक्तृभोग्यात्मकः कृत्स्नः प्रपञ्चस् तस्मात् प्रभवतीत्युक्तम्») without calling it an appearance, and he reads renunciation as giving up the fruits of action, not the rites; he states no school position. No Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s is not available here), so no position is given for those schools.

parallels.note: The opening half-verse, with the words in a different order and the compound dhātuprasādāt in the second half.

parallels.quote: सप्त प्राणाः प्रभवन्ति तस्मात्सप्तार्चिषः समिधः सप्त होमाः
parallels.note: The seven breaths; the Muṇḍaka has seven oblations (homāḥ) where this text has seven tongues.

parallels.quote: अतः समुद्रा गिरयश्च सर्वेऽस्मात्स्यन्दन्ते सिन्धवः सर्वरूपाः
parallels.note: The oceans, mountains and rivers; the Muṇḍaka continues with रसश्च and भूतैस्तिष्ठते ह्यन्तरात्मा.
The swan verse, word for word.
The ascetics sure of the Vedānta; the Muṇḍaka reads ब्रह्मलोकेषु and परामृताः.

parallels.quote: अथ यदिदमस्मिन्ब्रह्मपुरे दहरं पुण्डरीकं वेश्म दहरोऽस्मिन्नन्तराकाशः
parallels.note: The small lotus-house in the city of brahman and the space within it, cited here by Sāyaṇa.

contemporary.text: The anuvāka puts two practical ideas side by side: what lasts is not reached by accumulating — results, heirs, money — but by letting go; and attention can be turned to a small, quiet place within, where the commentators locate what is greatest. Many people today meet the same pair as a contrast between achievement and inner stillness. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What might it mean for something to be both smaller than the smallest and larger than the largest?
reflect.deeper: Sāyaṇa reads the four-horned bull as the syllable om; Bhāskara reads it as the sacrifice. What in the verse supports each reading?
reflect.practice: Sit for a few minutes with attention resting in the centre of the chest, and notice what the mind does when given so small a place to rest.

references.text: Several verses also occur in texts the edition’s parallel sources do not include: the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad has the first verse with dhātuḥ prasādāt (ŚU 3.20), the ajā verse (ŚU 4.5), the Rudra verse with viśvādhipaḥ and buddhyā śubhayā (ŚU 3.4, 4.12) and yasmāt paraṃ … vṛkṣa iva (ŚU 3.9); the Kaivalya Upaniṣad has na karmaṇā … tyāgenaike; and the ghee and bull verses are from the Ṛgveda’s fourth book (RV 4.58), outside the first book that the edition’s Ṛgveda source covers. They are noted here and not quoted.

Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara comment on this anuvāka as their tenth; the anonymous commentator as 10.12. Bhāskara refers the brahmā devānām and haṃsa verses to his comments elsewhere in the Āraṇyaka («ब्रह्मा देवानामिति ॥ व्याख्याता»).

flags.note: Printed forms kept so the padaccheda rejoins: उव् (the particle u), स्मृत्यास् (the commentators read स्मृत्या), विश्वाधियः (glossed विश्वाधिक; the Śvetāśvatara has विश्वाधिपः), परमेश्मभूतम् (Sāyaṇa वरवेश्म-, Bhāskara परवेश्म-), गुहाशयां, रसाच्च, विशोकः (Sāyaṇa विशोकं), गृद्ध्राणाग्.
Hiatus declared at sapta · ime, trayo · asya, hastāso · asya, tyāgenaike · amṛtatvam.
The ghee, bull and four-horn verses are read of brahman and om by Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator and of the sacrifice by Bhāskara; both readings are given.
